DataAudit.metaTitle: SMB Analytics Health Assessment — John Serra
DataAudit.metaDescription: A free five-minute assessment for small businesses to score analytics maturity, identify the biggest barrier, and get a practical action plan.

landing.headline: Can you trust the numbers running your business?
landing.intro: Find out whether your metrics, data, reporting, and ownership practices are strong enough to support confident decisions.
landing.privacyLabel: What you will not be asked for
landing.privacy: Do not share source exports, credentials, customer data, or other sensitive information. This assessment only asks about your business context and working practices.

context.title: First, tell us about the business.
context.intro: These four answers add context to the result. They do not change your score.

metrics.title: Metrics
metrics.intro: Consider whether the business has a shared, decision-ready definition of success.

data.title: Data
data.intro: Consider the completeness, accessibility, freshness, and consistency of the underlying records.

reporting.title: Reporting
reporting.intro: Consider whether reports are dependable and connected to a recurring decision process.

ownership.title: Ownership
ownership.intro: Consider whether people, access, documentation, and tools can survive normal business change.

questions.M1: We have an agreed list of five to seven numbers that represent the health of the business.
questions.M2: Each headline metric has a written definition, including what is included, excluded, and which time period it uses.
questions.M3: We know which system is the source of truth for each headline metric.
questions.M4: Each headline metric has a target or threshold connected to a specific action.
questions.M5: We can name a business decision from the last 90 days that changed because of what the data showed.
questions.D1: The transactions, leads, customers, and operational activity needed for our headline metrics are consistently captured.
questions.D2: We can export the detailed records behind our important numbers—not just view summaries or screenshots.
questions.D3: Our data covers the required period, is current enough for our decisions, and has no unexplained gaps.
questions.D4: Customer, transaction, product, and campaign records use reliable identifiers and consistent naming.
questions.D5: When an important number appears in two systems, we can explain and reconcile the difference.
questions.R1: We have one primary report or dashboard for the business rather than several competing versions.
questions.R2: The primary report is updated on schedule, displays its freshness, and requires little manual work.
questions.R3: Important numbers are shown against a target, prior period, or other meaningful comparison.
questions.R4: The team reviews the numbers at a recurring time—weekly or monthly.
questions.R5: Reviews produce documented actions with owners, and we later check whether those actions worked.
questions.O1: Every headline metric and important data source has a named owner.
questions.O2: The company controls access to its data and can retain it when an employee, agency, or vendor leaves.
questions.O3: Important reports and data workflows are documented well enough for another person to maintain.
questions.O4: At least one person in the company can troubleshoot or modify the primary report.
questions.O5: Our analytics tools are proportionate to the business, avoid unnecessary duplication, and support actual decisions.

flags.title: Check for urgent warning signs.
flags.intro: Answer based on what is true today. A “not sure” response is treated as a warning that needs verification.

questions.F1: Our revenue or customer total changes depending on which person or system is asked.
questions.F2: An agency, former employee, or vendor controls an account or dataset the business depends on.
questions.F3: Business-critical reporting depends on one undocumented spreadsheet or one person.
questions.F4: We are spending more on a marketing channel without independently connecting it to leads or sales.
questions.F5: We knowingly use a stale or broken report for important decisions.

errors.title: One more thing
errors.context: Choose an answer for all four business-context fields.
errors.questions: Answer all five statements before continuing.
errors.flags: Answer all five warning-sign statements before viewing your result.
errors.incomplete: Your score is not available until all 20 scored statements are answered.

barrierDescriptions.metrics: The business is collecting numbers without a sufficiently shared definition of which decisions those numbers should drive.
barrierDescriptions.data: A Data-Rich but Untrusted business has useful records, but gaps, access limits, or conflicting definitions weaken confidence in them.
barrierDescriptions.reporting: Reporting exists, but it is not consistently turning comparisons and reviews into owned, measurable action.
barrierDescriptions.ownership: Analytics depends too heavily on informal knowledge, fragile access, or tools without clear internal ownership.

profiles.verification: Several “not sure” answers mean verification should come before new analytics work.
profiles.optimization: The foundation is strong enough to focus on sharper decisions, faster feedback, and scale.
profiles.foundation: The priority is a dependable foundation: agreed metrics, trustworthy records, and a repeatable operating rhythm.

plan.title: Three moves, in priority order.
plan.intro: Complete these actions in sequence. The third may support a different pillar, but it was selected to strengthen the weakest part of your analytics system.

self_service.title: Build the core foundation first.
self_service.description: Use the plan as a focused internal checklist, then bring in help where ownership or data access remains blocked.

guided_diagnostic.title: Validate the weak link with a guided diagnostic.
guided_diagnostic.description: A short working session can test the assumptions behind the score and turn the plan into a scoped sequence of work.

implementation.title: Turn the plan into a reliable operating system.
implementation.description: Get hands-on help defining metrics, repairing the data path, and building reporting that produces action.

optimization.title: Optimize for faster, better decisions.
optimization.description: With the foundation in place, focus on sharper targets, less manual work, and a tighter feedback loop.

action_M1.title: Agree on the business health numbers
action_M1.why: A short shared list prevents teams from optimizing different versions of success.
action_M1.whatToDo: Choose five to seven headline numbers and record the decision each one supports.
action_M1.verify: Ask two leaders to name the list independently; their answers should match.

action_M2.title: Write a definition for every headline metric
action_M2.why: Written inclusion, exclusion, and time rules stop quiet interpretation drift.
action_M2.whatToDo: Create a one-page metric dictionary with formula, scope, time period, and owner.
action_M2.verify: Have two people calculate one metric from the definition and confirm the totals match.

action_M3.title: Assign a source of truth
action_M3.why: A named source prevents convenient system-switching when totals disagree.
action_M3.whatToDo: Map each headline metric to one authoritative system and the detailed table or export behind it.
action_M3.verify: Trace every dashboard total back to the recorded source without using screenshots.

action_M4.title: Connect every metric to a trigger
action_M4.why: A metric without a target or response cannot reliably change a decision.
action_M4.whatToDo: Set a target or threshold and document the action taken when it is missed or exceeded.
action_M4.verify: In the next review, record whether the trigger fired and what action followed.

action_M5.title: Prove that data changes decisions
action_M5.why: Analytics creates value only when evidence changes priorities, resources, or actions.
action_M5.whatToDo: Add a decision log to the recurring review and capture the evidence behind each material change.
action_M5.verify: Within 90 days, point to one logged decision and its measured outcome.

action_D1.title: Close critical capture gaps
action_D1.why: Missing transactions, leads, or activity make every downstream metric incomplete.
action_D1.whatToDo: List the records needed for headline metrics, then fix the highest-impact missing capture point.
action_D1.verify: Compare expected and captured record counts for a full operating cycle.

action_D2.title: Secure record-level exports
action_D2.why: Detailed records are necessary to test totals, investigate exceptions, and change tools safely.
action_D2.whatToDo: Confirm an authorized employee can export detailed data from each critical system in a usable format.
action_D2.verify: Produce and open a current export containing stable identifiers and dates.

action_D3.title: Test freshness, coverage, and gaps
action_D3.why: Decisions fail when data is late, covers the wrong period, or silently omits activity.
action_D3.whatToDo: Define freshness expectations and run checks for date coverage, missing periods, and unusual volume changes.
action_D3.verify: A scheduled check identifies a deliberately introduced late or missing batch.

action_D4.title: Standardize identifiers and names
action_D4.why: Reliable joins depend on stable IDs and consistent labels across systems.
action_D4.whatToDo: Choose canonical customer, transaction, product, and campaign identifiers and document naming rules.
action_D4.verify: Measure unmatched and duplicate records; both rates should fall after the change.

action_D5.title: Create a reconciliation rule
action_D5.why: Conflicting totals destroy trust unless timing and definition differences are explainable.
action_D5.whatToDo: After metric definitions are written, document how the two most important cross-system totals reconcile.
action_D5.verify: Reconcile a recent period to an agreed tolerance and explain every material difference.

action_R1.title: Choose one primary report
action_R1.why: A primary report creates a shared starting point without requiring new tracking software.
action_R1.whatToDo: Designate one existing report as primary and retire or clearly label competing versions.
action_R1.verify: Ask the review team which report governs; everyone should point to the same one.

action_R2.title: Make report freshness visible
action_R2.why: People cannot judge a report if its update time and manual dependencies are hidden.
action_R2.whatToDo: Display the last refresh time, document the update schedule, and remove one fragile manual step.
action_R2.verify: Observe two scheduled refreshes and confirm they complete on time with the date visible.

action_R3.title: Add decision-ready comparisons
action_R3.why: A number without a target or baseline gives no signal about whether action is needed.
action_R3.whatToDo: Add the most meaningful target, prior-period, or benchmark comparison to each headline view.
action_R3.verify: A reviewer can describe performance direction and gap without doing separate calculations.

action_R4.title: Set a recurring review rhythm
action_R4.why: Even a good report has little value if no one reviews it at a dependable time.
action_R4.whatToDo: Schedule a weekly or monthly review with a stable agenda, required attendees, and the primary report.
action_R4.verify: Complete three consecutive reviews on schedule and record attendance.

action_R5.title: Close the action loop
action_R5.why: Review meetings become reporting theater when actions have no owner or follow-up.
action_R5.whatToDo: Record each action, owner, due date, expected effect, and later outcome in a decision log.
action_R5.verify: At the next review, every prior action is closed, updated, or explicitly reassigned.

action_O1.title: Name metric and data owners
action_O1.why: Ownership makes definitions, quality issues, and access decisions someone’s explicit responsibility.
action_O1.whatToDo: Assign one accountable owner to every headline metric and critical data source.
action_O1.verify: Each owner confirms the role and can state the current issue or maintenance task.

action_O2.title: Put critical access under company control
action_O2.why: Vendor- or employee-owned accounts can interrupt operations and strand business data.
action_O2.whatToDo: Move billing, admin access, recovery methods, and exports for critical systems to company-controlled accounts.
action_O2.verify: An authorized second person can access, recover, and export from every critical system.

action_O3.title: Document the critical workflow
action_O3.why: Undocumented reports and pipelines create a single-person dependency.
action_O3.whatToDo: Document inputs, transformation steps, schedule, outputs, owners, and common failure recovery.
action_O3.verify: A second person follows the document to complete or troubleshoot one cycle.

action_O4.title: Build internal troubleshooting capacity
action_O4.why: The business needs a first responder when its primary report breaks or changes.
action_O4.whatToDo: Train one internal person to refresh, inspect, and make a small safe change to the primary report.
action_O4.verify: That person resolves a controlled test issue without relying on the original builder.

action_O5.title: Simplify the analytics toolset
action_O5.why: Duplicate or oversized tools add cost and inconsistent logic without improving decisions.
action_O5.whatToDo: Inventory analytics tools, the decision each supports, its owner, and overlapping capabilities; remove one unjustified duplicate.
action_O5.verify: Every retained tool has an active owner, a used output, and a documented business purpose.
